case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a sentence imposed under 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) must run consecutively to other sentences because § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) forbids concurrent sentences for terms imposed “under this subsection.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) (consecutive-sentencing mandate for terms imposed “under this subsection”) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) (causing death through use of a firearm “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Lora argues that § 924(j) is a separate offense with its own penalty provision, so a prison term imposed under § 924(j) is not imposed “under” § 924(c) and therefore is not subject to § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s mandatory consecutive-sentencing rule; instead, sentencing should proceed under ordinary discretion (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 3584), and any lingering uncertainty should be resolved in the defendant’s favor (rule of lenity).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States contends that § 924(j) incorporates a § 924(c) violation as an element (death caused through the use of a firearm in the course of violating § 924(c)), so a § 924(j) sentence necessarily rests on and functions as punishment for a § 924(c) offense; accordingly, the consecutive-sentencing command in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies, requiring the § 924(j) term to run consecutively to any other term, and the statute’s text/structure leaves no “grievous ambiguity” for lenity.

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point is Justice Alito’s anti-evasion concern, but under a minimalist approach we cannot extend a mandatory consecutive-sentencing command beyond what Congress clearly wrote. As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) by its terms applies only to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary drafting makes that subsection (c), while § 924(j) is separately codified with its own penalty provision—so importing (D)(ii) would expand punishment by implication. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Abbott and Dean reinforces that we treat § 924(c)’s sentencing architecture as attached to § 924(c) convictions, not silently carried into distinct offenses that borrow (c) as an element. The narrow, legitimacy-protecting resolution is to hold only that § 924(j) does not trigger (D)(ii), leaving § 3584(a) discretion and reserving broader charging-incentive questions for Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s anti-evasion argument has force as a policy matter, but it cannot override the enacted limitation in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” which, under ordinary hierarchical drafting, refers to subsection (c) and not subsection (j). The fact that § 924(j) requires a death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” means (c) supplies elements, not that (c)’s distinct sentencing command is imported into a different subsection with its own penalty clause. As Justice Kavanaugh notes, Abbott and Dean reinforce that we apply § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate where Congress attached it—i.e., to § 924(c) sentences—rather than extending it by implication to separate offenses. With § 924(j) silent, § 3584(a)’s default leaves concurrency to the sentencing court, and any doubt about expanding mandatory punishment should not be resolved in the government’s favor.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument is my own anti-evasion concern: that allowing § 924(j) sentences to run concurrently lets prosecutors bypass § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is textually limited to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary hierarchical drafting conventions make that subsection (c) rather than separately codified subsection (j) with its own penalty clause. Justice Kagan’s point is also persuasive that § 924(j)’s cross-reference to conduct “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” imports elements, not distinct sentencing commands; and Abbott and Dean, cited by Justice Kavanaugh, reinforce that we have treated § 924(c)’s mandatory consecutive architecture as cabined to § 924(c) convictions. On a textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, the policy worry cannot justify expanding a mandatory punishment rule by implication where Congress did not clearly displace § 3584(a)’s default discretion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Justice Alito’s anti-evasion concern—that prosecutors will charge § 924(j) to avoid § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate—but as Justice Kagan explains, that is a policy argument that cannot supply the clear statutory command needed to withdraw § 3584(a) discretion. The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s textual-structural point remains decisive: § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies only to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is a distinct subsection with its own penalty provision, so importing (D)(ii) would expand mandatory punishment by implication. Abbott and Dean, noted by Justice Kavanaugh, reinforce that we enforce § 924(c)’s mandatory features where Congress attached them—i.e., to § 924(c) sentences—rather than treating a cross-reference defining elements as silently carrying over separate sentencing rules. Given the real-world severity of mandatory consecutiveness in homicide cases, and the absence of clear notice in § 924(j), lenity and individualized sentencing considerations confirm the petitioner’s reading.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Justice Alito’s anti-evasion concern, but as he ultimately recognizes, that policy worry cannot justify extending a mandatory consecutive rule beyond Congress’s chosen words. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas are right that § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is textually limited to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary hierarchical drafting makes “this subsection” mean subsection (c), not the distinct offense-and-penalty scheme in subsection (j); (j)’s cross-reference to (c) supplies elements, not (c)’s separate sentencing command. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Abbott and Dean further supports cabining the consecutiveness mandate to § 924(c) sentences as written, leaving § 3584(a)’s default discretion to govern § 924(j) absent a clear withdrawal. Any residual circumvention risk is for Congress or charging policy to address, not for us to cure by implication in a criminal sentencing statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Justice Alito’s anti-evasion concern—that prosecutors could sidestep § 924(c) by charging § 924(j)—but that policy worry cannot justify extending a mandatory consecutive-sentencing command beyond the text Congress enacted. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies only to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary drafting makes that subsection (c), not the separate subsection (j) with its own penalty clause. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Abbott and Dean further supports keeping § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery tied to § 924(c) convictions rather than importing it by implication into a different offense; absent clear displacement, § 3584(a) supplies the default discretion and any lingering ambiguity is resolved by lenity. If circumvention is real, Congress can amend (j) to say so explicitly; we should not enlarge punishment by inference.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s anti-evasion concern is the strongest point for respondent, but under our text-and-structure approach it cannot justify extending a mandatory consecutive-sentencing command beyond the statute’s express boundary. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies only to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary drafting conventions make that subsection (c), not the separately codified § 924(j) with its own penalty scheme. Abbott and Dean, which several colleagues (including Justice Kagan) invoke, reinforce that we enforce § 924(c)’s sentencing architecture where Congress attached it—rather than importing it into distinct offenses by implication. With § 924(j) silent, § 3584(a) supplies the default of sentencing discretion, and any residual ambiguity should not be resolved to increase punishment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Justice Alito’s anti-circumvention concern—that prosecutors could evade § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate by charging § 924(j)—but that policy worry cannot supply text Congress did not enact. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is expressly limited to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary hierarchical drafting confines that to subsection (c), whereas § 924(j) is a distinct subsection with its own penalty provision. Abbott and Dean, noted by Justice Kavanaugh, reinforce the structural point that § 924(c)’s sentencing machinery (including consecutiveness) attaches to § 924(c) convictions, not to separate offenses that incorporate a (c) violation as an element. With § 924(j) silent, § 3584(a)’s default discretion remains, and we should not expand a mandatory sentencing command by implication in a criminal statute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument remains Justice Alito’s anti-evasion concern, but it cannot supply the clear statutory command needed to strip sentencing judges of § 3584(a) discretion, particularly in a criminal statute. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is textually limited to a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and ordinary drafting makes that subsection (c), not the distinct offense-and-penalty subsection (j). Abbott and Dean, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, describe the consecutive requirement as attached to “§ 924(c) sentences,” reinforcing that borrowing (c) as an element in (j) does not silently import (c)’s separate sentencing mandate. On a procedural-fairness and notice-focused approach, I cannot endorse expanding mandatory punishment by implication based on predictions about charging practices.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) bars concurrency only for a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is placed in a separate subsection with its own penalty provision, even though it references conduct occurring “in the course of a violation of subsection (c).” Read in the ordinary hierarchical way Congress drafts statutes, that text is best understood to limit the consecutive-sentencing mandate to sentences imposed under § 924(c) itself, leaving § 924(j) sentences subject to the default discretion in 18 U.S.C. § 3584 absent a clearer directive. Abbott v. United States underscores the Court’s textual, structure-based approach to § 924(c) sentencing rules and does not authorize extending § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate beyond the terms Congress said were imposed “under this subsection.” At minimum, given the severe consequences of mandatory stacking and the absence of an unmistakable command covering § 924(j), any residual ambiguity should not be resolved to expand punishment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) mandates consecutive sentences only for a term of imprisonment “imposed under this subsection,” and the ordinary meaning of “this subsection” refers to subsection (c) itself, not to a different subsection like § 924(j). Section 924(j) is codified as a separate offense with its own penalty provision and, while it incorporates a violation of § 924(c) as an element (“in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”), Congress did not extend subsection (c)’s consecutive-sentencing command to subsection (j) as it easily could have. Under the default rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3584(a), absent an express statutory command, the sentencing court retains discretion to impose concurrent or consecutive terms; importing § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) into § 924(j) would depart from the statute’s enacted text. This Court’s approach in Abbott v. United States, 562 U.S. 8 (2010), enforces § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate as written for § 924(c) sentences, not for sentences imposed under other subsections.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 924(j) applies only when the defendant, “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” causes death through the use of a firearm, so the punishment it authorizes necessarily rests on a proved § 924(c) violation and functions as an aggravated form of § 924(c) liability. Given Congress’s clear insistence that “no term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection shall run concurrently,” 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii), the most natural reading—considering structure and practical consequences—is that courts may not evade § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing command by charging the death-resulting variant in § 924(j). This Court’s § 924(c) cases treat the consecutive mandate as central to Congress’s scheme to ensure additional punishment for firearm use in violent and drug crimes, see Abbott v. United States, 562 U.S. 8, 12–13, 24–25 (2010), and that understanding supports applying the mandate where § 924(j) incorporates a § 924(c) violation as an element. Any ambiguity is not “grievous” enough to trigger lenity when the text and sentencing structure point toward consecutiveness and a contrary reading would undermine Congress’s evident law-enforcement objective.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) mandates consecutive sentences only for terms imposed “under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is a distinct offense and penalty provision enacted as a separate subsection that does not itself contain any consecutive-sentencing command. Because Congress knew how to impose mandatory consecutiveness and chose language expressly limited to subsection (c), ordinary sentencing discretion under 18 U.S.C. § 3584 governs § 924(j) sentences absent a clear directive to the contrary. The government’s incorporation theory reads “under this subsection” too broadly and would effectively add a severe mandatory rule to § 924(j) that Congress did not write, undermining individualized sentencing and creating harsh, categorical outcomes in serious cases. At minimum, any remaining ambiguity about whether a § 924(j) term is “under” § 924(c) should be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) mandates consecutiveness only for a term of imprisonment imposed “under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is a separate subsection that defines its own offense and penalty for causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c).” That cross-reference incorporates the (c) elements but does not import (c)’s distinct sentencing command, especially given Congress’s choice to place the homicide offense and its penalties in (j) rather than in (c). With § 924(j) silent on concurrency, ordinary sentencing discretion under 18 U.S.C. § 3584(a) governs; reading (D)(ii) to apply anyway would stretch “under this subsection” beyond its most natural textual boundary and create an unworkable overlay. The structure-focused approach reflected in Abbott v. United States, 562 U.S. 8 (2010), supports enforcing § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate where Congress expressly attached it, but not extending it to a different subsection absent clear text.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) bars concurrency only for a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is not “this subsection”: it is a separate subsection that defines its own offense and authorizes its own penalties for causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c).” Congress knows how to extend a consecutive-sentencing command to other subsections when it wishes, and the cross-reference in § 924(j) to a § 924(c) violation as an element does not transform a sentence imposed under § 924(j) into one imposed “under” § 924(c). Reading “under this subsection” to reach § 924(j) would stretch the text and risk collapsing distinct statutory provisions; at minimum, any residual uncertainty about the scope of a criminal consecutive-sentencing mandate should be resolved for the defendant under the rule of lenity. Dean v. United States underscores that § 924(c)’s sentencing rules must be applied as written, and here the written limitation—“under this subsection”—does not encompass § 924(j).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) requires consecutive sentences only for a term of imprisonment imposed “under this subsection,” i.e., under § 924(c) itself. By contrast, § 924(j) is codified as a separate subsection and supplies its own penalty provision for causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which incorporates a § 924(c) violation as an element but does not convert the resulting sentence into one imposed “under” § 924(c). Congress knew how to extend the consecutive-sentencing mandate beyond § 924(c) but did not do so here, and ordinary sentencing discretion under 18 U.S.C. § 3584 therefore governs; any residual ambiguity about the scope of “under this subsection” should not be resolved by expanding mandatory consecutive punishment. This reading also fits the Court’s approach in Dean v. United States, 581 U.S. 62 (2017), which treated § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate as targeted to sentences imposed under § 924(c) while preserving sentencing discretion elsewhere unless Congress clearly withdraws it.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) bars concurrent sentences only for terms imposed “under this subsection,” and under ordinary drafting conventions and this Court’s consistent usage that phrase refers to subsection (c) itself, not to a separate subsection like § 924(j). Section 924(j) is codified outside subsection (c) and supplies its own penalty scheme; while it incorporates a § 924(c) violation as an element (“in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”), Congress did not say the punishment is imposed “under” subsection (c), and we should not extend a consecutive-sentencing mandate beyond the text. Abbott v. United States and Dean v. United States confirm that § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing rules operate by the terms Congress enacted for sentences imposed under § 924(c), not by implication for distinct offenses that reference § 924(c). At minimum, any residual uncertainty about whether § 924(j) triggers § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) should be resolved in favor of ordinary sentencing discretion under 18 U.S.C. § 3584, consistent with the rule of lenity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) bars concurrent sentences only for a “term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is codified as a distinct subsection with its own penalty provision for causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” not a sentence imposed “under” subsection (c) itself. This Court’s descriptions of the consecutive-sentencing mandate in Abbott v. United States and Greenlaw v. United States repeatedly tie the bar to “§ 924(c) convictions” and “§ 924(c) sentences,” confirming the limitation to subsection (c) rather than cross-referenced offenses like (j). Treating § 924(j) as implicitly subject to § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing command would expand punishment without clear congressional direction, undermining procedural fairness and, at minimum, triggering the rule of lenity in the face of ambiguity. Accordingly, sentencing discretion should proceed under the ordinary framework of 18 U.S.C. § 3584, rather than a mandatory consecutive rule imported from § 924(c).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the mandatory consecutive-sentencing rule in 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies when the defendant is convicted and sentenced under 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) for a death caused through the use of a firearm in the course of a § 924(c) violation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) (consecutive sentencing for terms imposed 'under this subsection') and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) (penalties when, in the course of a § 924(c) violation, death is caused through firearm use).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Lora argues that § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) by its plain text applies only to a 'term of imprisonment imposed ... under this subsection'—i.e., under § 924(c) itself—whereas a conviction under § 924(j) imposes a sentence under § 924(j), a different subsection with its own penalty scheme. Because Congress chose not to include an express consecutive-sentencing command in § 924(j), sentencing courts retain discretion to run a § 924(j) sentence concurrently with other sentences. Lora also invokes structural and policy considerations (preserving judicial sentencing discretion and avoiding prosecutor-driven stacking) and, to the extent any ambiguity remains, the rule of lenity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States contends that § 924(j) is best understood as operating through § 924(c): it criminalizes causing death 'in the course of' violating § 924(c) and therefore incorporates § 924(c)'s sentencing features, including the consecutive-sentencing mandate in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii). The government argues the statutory text, structure, and purpose show no 'grievous ambiguity,' making lenity inapplicable, and notes that most circuits have held § 924(j) sentences must be consecutive.

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that § 924(j) occurs “in the course of” a § 924(c) violation and therefore should inherit § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing rule—cannot overcome the express limitation in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” which is subsection (c), not (j). Justice Thomas’s focus on that limiting phrase is decisive for a minimalist disposition: we can resolve the case on the narrow textual ground that Congress did not extend the consecutive command beyond (c), without opining on broader sentencing policy. Justice Alito’s Setser point appropriately supplies the baseline—absent a clear statutory directive, § 3584 leaves concurrency to the district court—and nothing in § 924(j)’s standalone penalty provision clearly withdraws that discretion. Abbott’s repeated linkage of mandatory consecutiveness to “§ 924(c) sentences,” as Justice Kagan notes, reinforces that our precedents treat the mandate as subsection-specific rather than an attribute that automatically follows any cross-reference to (c).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that § 924(j)’s reference to causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” should import § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing command, but that reading ignores Congress’s limiting words: § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies only to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” i.e., subsection (c). As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Congress knows how to draft a consecutive mandate that reaches beyond a single subsection, and it did not do so here; importing (c)’s sentencing rule into (j) would effectively rewrite “this subsection” to mean “this section.” Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on ordinary code hierarchy (Koons Buick) reinforces the textual point that “subsection” is not a free-floating cross-reference. Abbott’s repeated framing of the rule as tied to § 924(c) convictions and sentences further supports limiting the mandate to sentences imposed under (c), and any residual doubt in a penalty provision counsels against expanding mandatory punishment without clear text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that § 924(j)’s “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” imports all of § 924(c), including mandatory consecutiveness—still cannot overcome the limiting language in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applying only to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, rewriting “this subsection” to mean “this section” is not a permissible move in a criminal penalty statute, especially when Congress readily could have drafted a broader command. Justice Gorsuch’s Koons Buick hierarchy point reinforces that “subsection” is a precise internal reference, not a free-floating incorporation device, and Abbott’s repeated framing of the rule as tied to “§ 924(c) sentences” supports keeping the consecutiveness mandate cabined to sentences actually imposed under (c). Setser and § 3584 supply the sensible default: absent a clear directive in (j), district courts retain discretion over concurrency, and nothing in (j)’s standalone penalty provision clearly withdraws it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that § 924(j)’s “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” imports all of § 924(c)’s sentencing incidents—cannot overcome the explicit limiter in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection.” Justice Kagan’s textual/structural point is decisive: a sentence imposed under subsection (j), which has its own penalty scheme, is not a sentence imposed “under” subsection (c), so the consecutive mandate doesn’t attach. Justice Alito’s reliance on Setser reinforces the baseline that, absent a clear congressional command, district courts retain discretion over concurrency—a safeguard that matters acutely where § 924(j) already authorizes extreme punishment and mandatory stacking would create rigid, potentially disproportionate outcomes. Abbott’s repeated linkage of consecutiveness to “§ 924(c) sentences,” as the Chief Justice notes, supports cabining the mandate to subsection (c) rather than expanding punishment by inference.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that § 924(j) occurs “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so Congress must have meant to carry over all of (c)’s sentencing attributes, including mandatory consecutiveness. But that inference runs headlong into the limiting text Justice Roberts emphasizes: § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) bars concurrency only for a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” and (j) is a different subsection with its own penalty scheme, so the sentence is imposed “under” (j), not (c). Justice Alito’s Setser point strengthens the baseline: absent a clear statutory command, concurrency remains within ordinary sentencing discretion, and nothing in (j) supplies the missing directive. Abbott’s repeated linkage of the consecutive mandate to “§ 924(c) sentences” supports reading the mandate as subsection-bound rather than a free-floating feature that attaches to any offense referencing (c).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 924(j) is committed “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so (j) should inherit (c)’s consecutive-sentencing rule; but that treats an element cross-reference as if it were a penalty cross-reference, contrary to the enacted text. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) limits its command to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” and under ordinary hierarchical drafting (and the baseline Setser framework Justice Alito notes), a sentence imposed under subsection (j) is not a sentence “under” subsection (c). Abbott’s repeated linkage of the consecutive mandate to “§ 924(c) sentences” reinforces that our precedents describe the rule as subsection-bound, not a free-floating incident of any offense that mentions (c). Any residual uncertainty in a criminal penalty provision should be resolved by lenity rather than by expanding mandatory stacking beyond Congress’s clear words.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention remains that § 924(j)’s “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” language should import § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing rule, but that treats an element cross-reference as a penalty command and cannot overcome Congress’s express limitation to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection.” Chief Justice Roberts’s ordinary-meaning/hierarchy point is decisive: “this subsection” in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) refers to subsection (c) itself, and extending it to (j) would effectively rewrite the statute to say “this section,” which we should not do in a criminal sentencing provision. Justice Alito’s Setser framing reinforces the baseline that, absent a clear directive, § 3584 leaves concurrency to district-court discretion—and § 924(j)’s standalone penalty provision supplies no clear withdrawal of that discretion. Abbott’s repeated tethering of the mandate to “§ 924(c) sentences,” as Justice Thomas notes, supports keeping the consecutiveness rule cabined to sentences actually imposed under (c), not exported to a different subsection.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that § 924(j) incorporates all of § 924(c)’s sentencing incidents because death occurs “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”—still treats an element cross-reference as a penalty cross-reference, and the text does not support that move. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is expressly limited to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” which in ordinary hierarchical drafting means subsection (c), not a separate subsection (j) with its own penalty provision. Justice Alito’s invocation of Setser reinforces that, absent a clear statutory withdrawal, district courts retain concurrency discretion under § 3584, and § 924(j) contains no clear consecutive command. Abbott and Dean describe the consecutive mandate as attached to § 924(c) sentences; extending it to (j) would effectively rewrite “this subsection” to “this section,” a step we should not take in a criminal sentencing statute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that § 924(j)’s “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” should import all of (c)’s sentencing incidents—reads an element cross-reference as an unstated penalty command, and it cannot overcome the express limiter in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection.” Justice Kagan’s structural argument is most persuasive to me: Congress placed (j) in a separate subsection with its own penalty scheme and omitted any consecutive directive, which strongly signals that ordinary § 3584 discretion remains. Justice Alito’s Setser framing reinforces the baseline that concurrency is the default absent a clear withdrawal of discretion, and Abbott’s repeated focus on “§ 924(c) sentences” supports cabining the consecutive mandate to sentences actually imposed under (c). Given the practical liberty consequences of mandatory stacking, I would not infer an additional penalty constraint without clearer text, and any residual ambiguity favors the defendant under lenity.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) mandates consecutiveness only for a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” and the ordinary meaning of “this subsection” is subsection (c), not a different subsection like § 924(j) with its own penalty scheme. Reading § 924(j) to import § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing rule would require extending a sentencing mandate beyond the text Congress chose, even though Congress elsewhere shows it knows how to make a consecutive-sentencing command apply across subsections when it wants to. Our § 924(c) cases—most notably Abbott v. United States—treat the consecutiveness command as tied to sentences imposed under § 924(c) itself, reinforcing a narrow, text-bound application rather than an implied cross-subsection incorporation. Any remaining uncertainty about whether § 924(j) silently carries § 924(c)’s mandatory consecutive rule is resolved against expanding punishment beyond clear statutory authorization.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The consecutive-sentencing command in 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies only to a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” and § 924(j) is a different subsection that sets out its own penalties for causing death “in the course of” a § 924(c) violation. Reading the text as written respects Congress’ subsection-specific choice of language; had Congress meant § 924(j) sentences to be mandatory consecutive, it could have said so in § 924(j) itself. This Court’s decisions repeatedly describe the consecutive-sentencing rule as tied to “§ 924(c) conviction[s]” and “§ 924(c) sentences,” not to separate offenses outside that subsection. See Abbott v. United States, 562 U.S. 8, 12–13, 24–25 (2010); consistent with that textual approach, any lingering ambiguity in a criminal penalty should be resolved against expanding punishment absent clear congressional command.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) mandates consecutiveness only for a “term of imprisonment imposed … under this subsection,” and a sentence for a § 924(j) conviction is imposed under subsection (j), which contains its own penalty scheme and no express consecutive-sentencing command. Reading “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” in § 924(j) to import all of § 924(c)’s sentencing rules stretches the text beyond what Congress actually said and effectively rewrites “under this subsection” to mean “under this section,” contrary to ordinary textualist interpretation. Under Setser v. United States, 566 U.S. 231 (2012), courts retain discretion over concurrent versus consecutive sentencing absent a clear statutory directive, and § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s clear directive does not, by its terms, reach § 924(j). The practical consequence is not to excuse violent conduct—§ 924(j) authorizes severe punishment up to death—but simply to preserve the sentencing discretion Congress did not clearly remove for subsection (j).

This Court’s descriptions in Abbott v. United States treat § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing rule as tied to a “§ 924(c) conviction” and “§ 924(c) sentence,” reinforcing that the mandate does not silently attach to sentences imposed under a different subsection. Reading § 924(j) to import § 924(c)’s consecutive mandate would expand punishment without clear statutory authorization and unduly constrain sentencing courts’ ability to impose fair, individualized sentences in cases already carrying the most severe penalties. At minimum, any residual uncertainty in this cross-subsection sentencing question should be resolved in favor of discretion rather than mandatory stacking.

Our descriptions of the consecutive-sentencing command in Abbott repeatedly tie the bar to “§ 924(c) conviction[s]” and “§ 924(c) sentences,” reinforcing that the mandate is not a free-floating feature that automatically attaches to other offenses. Given that textual and structural coherence, sentencing courts retain discretion to run § 924(j) sentences concurrently, without needing to invoke lenity.
